title: Duke's physical temper: Ben Webster, Hodges against the wall and ashtrays at Cootie
summary: Stories of union representatives at the Sherman Hotel, Duke holding Hodges against a wall and throwing ashtrays at Cootie Williams.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well, one time I think they had a problem. It was in Chicago and they were working the Sherman Hotel, and you had to come off the stand in one wing or the other. It was something like a stage, you know, at intermission. And Ben kept standing in the wings and he wouldn't allow Duke to come off the stand. So what they did, they called up the union representatives, and the union representatives used to carry little guns under their coats. And that made --
Just in Chicago or other places, too?

Well, I know this happened in Chicago, but I don't know about other places. Then there was one time when Duke began to show his temper, physically you know, really, and it scared Ben, because Duke had been walking around so cool all the time, and he didn't realize that Duke would get mad and do the same thing, you know? Because there was another time when I think Johnny Hodges was mad at Duke about something, and you know Johnny Hodges was short.
Uh-huh.
He called Duke a name that Duke didn't
like, and Duke picked him up, you know, like beside a wall, and held him up, and Johnny's feet were dangling off the ground.
Oh, gee.
He said, "Nobody calls me that."
Who?
Duke said that.
Uh-huh.
You know, he was mad at Johnny. And Johnny, no, he never said it again.
That's as far as it went, though, he just picked him up and let him dangle. He didn't hit him or anything.

No, no, he didn't hit him. He just picked him up, like a wall -- like he didn't hold him up, he balanced him up beside of a wall, you know. And there was another time, I think they were rehearsing, and Duke was very concerned about this arrangement, and I guess everybody knows how Cat Anderson and Cootie Williams did not get along. But they were rehearsing where there was a stack of empty ashtrays close to Duke, and Cootie was -- I don't know, he was in one of those moods where he didn't feel like playing what Duke wanted, and Duke started throwing ashtrays like you throw those little sailor things, you know? And Cat Anderson said -- the way Cat described it, he said -- you know he called Duke Piano Red, you know -- Cat says he grabbed his horn and ran, because Piano Red might miss
his mark and hit him.
(Laughter)
He was really throwing at Cootie, you know.
(Laughter)
Was he like throwing to hit, I mean aiming to --
Yeah, he was throwing it right at him, you know.
Serious.

Yeah, he was very serious. Cootie kept on foiling around with some chart he'd written, and he meant -- he'd called the rehearsal because he was serious about it. And Cootie didn't feel like -- but that night, the first guy in his chair and [very orderly,] like a Boy Scout, was Cootie Williams.
(Laughter)
Because Duke -- see, they never expected Duke to get, you know, showing his temper like that. But he did, because he'd been so cool for so many years, you know. Apparently cool.
He seemed to have more of a short temper in his later years.
Yes, he did.
Than he ever did before.

I noticed it when we were doing "My People." It wasn't temper at that point, but it was -- he was very authoritative, you know, because he used to say he was not a disciplinarian. But he wanted discipline on that project, and he wasn't kidding.
Yeah.
We had to really work.
